content_metadata.description: An insightful interview with Mariana Costa Checa, Co-founder and CEO of Laboratoria, discussing the organization's mission, growth, and impact.

qAndA.answer: Mariana noticed the lack of female developers while building her own software development company in Lima.
qAndA.question: What prompted Mariana to explore solutions for the underrepresentation of women in tech?

qAndA.answer: Many developers did not have formal computer science degrees, highlighting that software development could be inclusive.
qAndA.question: What is unique about the educational backgrounds of the developers Mariana initially hired?

qAndA.answer: 'Soft skills' like teamwork, communication, and self-learning are crucial for success in tech.
qAndA.question: Why does Laboratoria prioritize life skills alongside coding skills?

qAndA.answer: Focuses on group work, continuous feedback through retrospectives, and self-directed learning.
qAndA.question: How does Laboratoria's 'Agile Classroom' methodology work?

qAndA.answer: The video conveys hope and excitement with an optimistic and inspiring tone.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Mariana mentions her initial venture as a software development company and the challenge of finding skilled developers, especially women.
Mariana shares the difficulty of finding female developers and how her own experience as a minority in her company inspired her to explore solutions.
Mariana describes the widespread underrepresentation of women in the tech sector across different companies and events.
Mariana talks about the diverse educational backgrounds of developers in her company and how software development could be more inclusive.
Mariana recounts running a pilot program to train women in software development to address the need for more women developers in her company.
Mariana concludes by stating that the pilot program's success led to the creation of Laboratoria.

Mariana emphasizes the importance of teamwork, communication, and feedback skills for success in the tech industry.
Mariana details Laboratoria's methodology, "The Agile Classroom," which incorporates agile principles and values of software development to foster life skills development.
Mariana describes how the program focuses on group work, continuous retrospectives, self-learning, and challenges traditional teaching methods.
Mariana concludes that Laboratoria's holistic approach prepares women to face the competitive tech sector.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Mariana acknowledges their expansion to Santiago, Mexico City, and Guadalajara, reflecting on the decision's boldness and the motivation from her friends.
Mariana highlights the realization that Laboratoria's model works in any large city with a growing tech sector and women seeking opportunities.
Mariana acknowledges the challenges of scaling the organization while maintaining quality and culture.
Mariana expresses pride in Laboratoria's growth and the program's evolution through experiences in different centers and teams.
Mariana emphasizes the impact of Laboratoria in creating a sense of belonging among students and alumni.
Mariana expresses excitement for her TEDx talk in Geneva, where she will focus on the importance of diversity and inclusion in tech and how Laboratoria contributes to shaping the world's future.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We are a social enterprise that's working to give thousands of women in Latin America the skills they need to build a career in the tech sector.
We do this because the tech sector is growing, there's a lot of job opportunities and it desperately needs not only talent but diverse talent.
It's a sector that traditionally has had a very small presence of women and it's very important to change that because technologies used by men and women almost equally.
If we want that technology to be able to solve for our needs too, we need more women creating technology.
It's a very important thing to do.
It's funny because I think it often happens when one starts in this entrepreneurial journey.
I didn't start with La Guardatoria. My co-founders and I actually started a software development company before.
We were doing software developments for all sorts of clients and we had to build our own team.
That's how we came up on the problem that it was actually hard to find good developers out there.
This was in Lima back in 2013 and it was almost impossible to find any women.
Our company started growing and I started becoming more and more of a minority.
There were no women in our software development team.
Maybe we were around 15 people and it was just me and a graphic designer.
I started thinking this is interesting. I don't understand why it's in the case and I think we can do something to change that.
It was not only that reality in our company. This is what you would see in any other company doing software in any software development meetup, in communities.
It was very widespread.
The other thing that I saw that was pretty unique of the world of software is that it's a space where I think traditional education is being challenged in many ways.
Half of the developers in our team did not come from a formal five-year degree in computer science.
The best one had learned by himself.
Completely. Others had learned in communities. Others had studied something else and then randomly ended up in software.
It had the potential to be a very inclusive space.
That's when initially to solve our own needs of having more developers and specifically more women developers,
we ran a pilot program to see if we could actually prepare in a relatively short period of time of six months.
We started to be ready to start working with us.
That's when we discovered that a whole new world of opportunity and laboratory was born.
Yes, completely. I think that life skills are what people traditionally call the soft skills that are actually the hardest ones to get.
They will be the most important skills in the future.
Since the beginning, we said it's actually not enough to get someone that knows the technical part.
If they're not going to be able to work in teams, if they're not going to be able to communicate properly, to give and receive feedback, it's not going to work out.
We designed the learning experience in a way in which the building of those life skills is ingrained in how they learn technology.
We have a methodology that we call the agile classroom.
The agile values of software development are like the gold standard of how to develop software.
We try to bring those to the learning experience.
There's a lot of group work. There's a focus on continuous retrospective.
I'm thinking, what could I have done better? There's a very strong focus on self-learning.
We actually barely have any classes, which at the beginning is always shocking for our students.
They're like, where's my teacher? What's the lesson?
We're like, that's not how it's going to work here.
Because we think that's the way to prepare them holistically to really face the challenges of a very competitive sector.
We started in Lima and then relatively early on with scales to Santiago, a Chilean Mexico City.
Looking back, it was probably a very irresponsible decision.
But really two of my greatest friends were there and they wanted to partner with us and see if there was potential for something like laboratory adhere.
I think very early on we realized that in any big city that has a growing tech sector and where you have women looking for better opportunity, laboratory works.
So we scaled and then we continued.
So now we have five centers. Lima, Santiago, Mexico, Guadalajara and São Paulo.
I think it's been of course challenging because it means a bigger organization, how do we ensure quality and culture and so on.
But it's been amazing. I think it's enabled us to build a program that has grown and nurtured from all these different realities.
And it has become better with the experience of every single center and every team.
And I think it gives us as a team, but also our students are an alumni, the feeling of being part of something big.
This is a movement that grows Latin America that's transforming the sector.
Yes, I'm very excited about that.
I am going to be talking about the story of how laboratory that was born, what we do and why it is important.
I will talk a lot about diversity and inclusion and how it is really imminent that we get more women and more minorities into building tech.
that's the only way in which we're going to make sure that we are also part of
designing the world's future.
